title: Genesis 11. The Cup Scattered.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 11. The Cup Scattered.
The whole earth had one language and one speech.
They traveled east and found a plain in the land of Shinar.
They settled there.
They said to one another: Come, let us make bricks,
and burn them thoroughly.
They had brick for stone and tar for mortar.
Then they said: Come, let us build ourselves a city,
and a tower whose top reaches to the heavens,
and let us make a name for ourselves,
lest we be scattered over the face of the whole earth.
The Cup tries to rise.
Not by God filling it, by man building upward.
This is the inversion of everything Genesis has shown.
God speaks, and creation receives.
God pours down; man builds up.
God gives a name; man makes one for himself.
God scatters; man gathers.
The same word, come,
that God used in chapter seven when He said to Noah,
"Come into the ark," is now used by man: Come,
let us build.
The invitation that once led to salvation now leads to a tower.
They know the command.
Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth.
They say it themselves, lest we be scattered.
They are building against the blessing.
The Cup that was meant to pour out into every nation is being gathered into one city,
one tower, one name.
The Lord comes down to see the city and the tower which the children of man had built.
The tower whose top reaches to the heavens,
God has to come down to even see it.
The gap between what man builds and where God dwells is revealed by the descent.
The tower that was meant to reach heaven does not reach God's feet.
He must descend to inspect it.
The same language of descent that was used in chapter three,
God walking in the garden, is used here.
God comes down.
But this time He does not come to walk.
He comes to see what man has made of himself.
God says: Behold, they are one people,
and they all have one language,
and this is what they begin to do.
Now nothing will be withheld from them that they intend to do.
This is not fear.
God is not threatened.
He is diagnosing.
The unity that was given, one language, one people,
has become the engine of autonomous ambition.
What they begin to do will not stop at a tower.
The Cup that was one vessel is being filled with a single intention:
to make a name for themselves.
The unity that was a gift is now being used against the Giver.
Come, let Us go down, and there confuse their language,
that they may not understand one another's speech.
God uses the same words they used.
They said: Come, let us build.
God says: Come, let Us go down.
The invitation that man directed upward, God redirects downward.
What man gathered, God scatters.
What man unified by brick and tar, God divides by language.
Not by destruction, by confusion.
The Cup is not shattered.
It is scattered.
The vessel is not broken.
It is divided into vessels that cannot understand each other.
They stop building the city.
The tower stands unfinished.
The name they tried to make for themselves is replaced by a name God gives:
Babel, because there the Lord confused the language of all the earth.
The name man wanted for himself becomes the name of his confusion.
From there the Lord scattered them over the face of all the earth.
The scattering they feared becomes the scattering God enacts.
The blessing of chapter nine, fill the earth, is fulfilled,
but through judgment.
What man refused to do in obedience, God accomplishes in confusion.
The Cup that was one is now many, divided by language,
separated by land, scattered across the face of the earth.
The division already noted as fact in chapter ten is now shown as event in chapter eleven.
Then the line narrows.
This is the history of the generations of Shem.
Two years after the flood,
Shem is a hundred years old and fathers Arpachshad.
The names descend, Arpachshad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor, Terah.
The genealogy moves faster than chapter five.
No ages at death.
No "and he died.
The drumbeat has been replaced by a current.
The Cup is not pausing to mourn.
It is moving toward someone.
Terah lives seventy years and fathers Abram, Nahor, and Haran.
Haran fathers Lot.
Then Haran dies before his father Terah,
in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldees.
A father buries a son.
The pattern of chapter four, Abel dead, a brother left, echoes here.
But the line does not stop.
Abram and Nahor take wives.
Abram's wife is Sarai.
Nahor's wife is Milcah, the daughter of Haran.
Sarai was barren.
She had no child.
The Cup that has carried life through creation, through flood, through scattering,
reaches a woman who cannot bear.
The line that has produced nations now ends in a womb that is closed.
Everything that has been preserved, the image, the breath, the covenant,
the promise,
arrives at a man with a barren wife in a city where his brother died.
Terah takes Abram, Lot, and Sarai.
They set out from Ur of the Chaldees to go to the land of Canaan.
They come to Haran and settle there.
Terah's days are two hundred and five years.
Terah dies in Haran.
The family that set out for Canaan stopped short.
The father who began the journey did not finish it.
He left Ur.
He never reached the land he was traveling toward.
He settled in a place that bore his dead son's name.
The Cup is scattered across nations.
But inside the scattering, one family has been singled out.
A man with a barren wife.
A nephew whose father is dead.
A family that stopped halfway.
The next move will not be Terah's.
The next move will be God's.
